section_summary: This section documents U.S. debate and policy concerning exports that could sustain Japan’s military industry, including petroleum technology, aviation fuel, scrap iron, copper, cryolite, and other strategic materials. It combines public appeals for broader embargoes with intelligence reports on Japanese procurement methods, diplomatic reporting on shipments from Latin America and Canada, and internal State Department deliberations. Particular attention is given to oil-refining plans requested from Universal Oil Products, suspected efforts to evade export controls, and proposals to aid China while restricting Japan’s access to American resources.

subfiles.title: Herbert C. Jones letter forwarding newspaper clippings on war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Jones forwards three newspaper clippings concerning the supply of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jones tells Hull that the enclosed clippings reflect public concern over furnishing Japan with war materials. They include a Washington Merry-Go-Round column and editorials or articles from the San Jose Mercury Herald and San Francisco Chronicle.

subfiles.title: Reply to Herbert C. Jones
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Jones’s clippings and says the issue is under careful government consideration.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Jones for his October 2 communication and its three clippings. He states that all interested branches of the government are carefully considering shipments of war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal to Adolf A. Berle Jr.
subfiles.about: Hoover transmits FBI information concerning suspected Japanese procurement activity.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle data that may interest the State Department. The enclosure is the FBI report that follows on Japanese and other foreign efforts to obtain petroleum technology and aviation fuel.

subfiles.title: FBI report: Megata; Akiyama; Okura Company—Espionage
subfiles.from: F. I. McGarraghy, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The report describes alleged Japanese, German, Italian, and Soviet attempts to obtain high-octane fuel, refinery plans, and petroleum-processing knowledge in the United States.
subfiles.summary: A confidential informant alleges that Japanese companies acting for the Japanese Navy used ostensibly civilian projects and other subterfuges to acquire oil-cracking plans and evade export restrictions. The report reproduces company memoranda about Japanese Army and industry delegations seeking American refinery, alkylation, hydrogenation, and aviation-gasoline technology. It also discusses German and Soviet procurement contacts, an alleged plan to route Phillips Petroleum gasoline to Germany through Japan, and Okura Company’s dealings with American industrial firms. The FBI closes the case because it found no evidence of a federal-law violation, while forwarding copies of plans supplied to Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: State Department response to the Attorney General concerning the FBI report
subfiles.about: The Department recommends continued surveillance of Okura Company for possible export-control evasion.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary acknowledges Hoover’s transmittal of the McGarraghy report and encloses presidential proclamations and regulations governing petroleum products, tetraethyl lead, scrap metal, and aviation-fuel technology. The Department believes Okura Company may previously have tried to evade restrictions and may continue trying to obtain controlled equipment, plans, and specifications. It recommends watching the company for two or three months under the Export Control Act.

subfiles.title: Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company inquiry about cryolite exports
subfiles.about: Beale asks whether his company should stop supplying Japan with cryolite used to manufacture aluminum.
subfiles.summary: Beale explains that Japan formerly obtained cryolite from Copenhagen and that his company may now be the only source of natural cryolite available to Japanese aluminum producers. Although one shipment has already been made, the company hesitates to continue if the aluminum would be used in aircraft or other war machinery. He offers voluntary cooperation despite the absence of an apparent legal prohibition.

subfiles.title: Internal note on proposed cryolite reply
subfiles.from: C. W. Y., Division of Controls
subfiles.about: The note records that the company president wants a State Department letter supporting refusal to sell cryolite to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cumming reports that Pennsylvania Salt’s president desires a letter of the proposed kind. Such a response would allow him to justify refusing Japanese purchases of cryolite.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning cryolite exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The Department indicates that selling cryolite for Japanese aluminum manufacture would conflict with the President’s moral-embargo statement.
subfiles.summary: The reply encloses the President’s December 1939 statement against exporting materials essential to aircraft manufacture to countries bombing civilians. It advises that the proposed cryolite exports would not accord with that policy and thanks the company for offering to cooperate.

subfiles.title: Report of proposed Seaboard Railway scrap-iron sale
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports negotiations to sell 22,000 tons of scrap iron to Japanese interests before an expected embargo.
subfiles.summary: John Blair Moffett telephoned with information that the Seaboard Railway was arranging a rapid sale of scrap iron, probably to Mitsui. According to his source, the parties were hurrying because they expected an imminent embargo on scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Shanghai telegram on measures to hamper Japanese war industry
subfiles.from: Butrick, American Consulate General at Shanghai
subfiles.about: The telegram recommends selective industrial obstruction instead of conspicuous general embargoes.
subfiles.summary: Qualified observers propose delaying critical plant components, withholding carbon electrodes and lubricating-oil solvents, refusing American installation technicians, and intensifying inspections of Japanese ships and cargoes. They argue that such measures would damage Japanese industry without giving militarists the propaganda benefits of a formal embargo. One observer believes only a complete oil embargo would drive Japan toward warlike action against the Dutch East Indies.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Shanghai recommendations on industrial restrictions
subfiles.about: This confidential paraphrase restates proposed measures for obstructing Japanese industry without a broad embargo.
subfiles.summary: The document recommends withholding technical personnel, solvents, essential plant parts, and carbon electrodes while rigorously inspecting Japanese vessels. Observers believe Japan has enough aviation fuel for current operations and could use lower-grade gasoline except when starting aircraft. They warn that a complete American oil embargo might prompt an attack on the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of W. L. Harding’s letter
subfiles.about: A Senate form refers Harding’s communication to the Department for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: The communication is transmitted with thanks for whatever favorable consideration it warrants. The Department is asked to return the enclosure with its report.

subfiles.title: W. L. Harding letter on possible Mexican transshipment of scrap iron
subfiles.about: Harding warns that an embargo on scrap exports to Japan might be evaded by trucking iron into Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Harding asks whether scrap could be sold to Mexico and then resold to Japan after the expected October 16 embargo. He suggests limiting American iron exports to Canada and expresses support for England’s war effort.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Sheppard concerning indirect exports
subfiles.about: Hull says the Department and other agencies are studying indirect shipment problems.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Sheppard’s referral of Harding’s warning about indirect exports through third countries. He says the issue and related problems are receiving careful interagency study and returns the constituent’s letter.

subfiles.title: Washington Committee for Aid to China questionnaire to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Dudley P. Babcock, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: The committee asks Roosevelt to state his position on embargoes against Japan and additional assistance to China and Britain.
subfiles.summary: The committee condemns the contradiction between criticizing Japanese aggression and supplying Japan’s war machine. It asks whether Roosevelt favors an immediate administrative or statutory embargo, how the United States should respond to Japanese procurement elsewhere in the Americas, and whether he supports more aid to China and Britain. It also asks about improving relations with the Soviet Union to keep it from joining the Axis.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Dudley P. Babcock
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges the committee’s foreign-policy questionnaire without answering its specific questions.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that Babcock’s October 4 letter to the President was referred to the State Department. He assures Babcock that the government is giving constant and earnest attention to the international situation and the matters raised.

subfiles.title: Luther A. Johnson letter forwarding F. H. Winslow’s embargo appeal
subfiles.about: Johnson forwards a constituent’s appeal for an embargo on Japan, Germany, and Italy.
subfiles.summary: Johnson says Winslow presents a forceful case for an embargo, especially against Japan. He adds that many other Texans have written similarly and asks Hull to consider their viewpoint.

subfiles.title: Reply to Luther A. Johnson
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Winslow’s views and Johnson’s assessment of Texas opinion.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Johnson for forwarding the letter and notes Johnson’s belief that it represents many patriotic Texans. The Winslow letter is returned for Johnson’s files.

subfiles.title: Bruce Barton letter forwarding the Stettens’ appeal
subfiles.about: Barton forwards a constituent communication calling for an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Barton describes the enclosed message from Dr. and Mrs. DeWitt Stetten as self-explanatory. The enclosure asks for an end to all exports to Japan and action against surplus German diplomatic personnel.

subfiles.title: DeWitt Stettens’ appeal for a complete export embargo
subfiles.about: The Stettens request a total embargo on exports to Japan and the recall of excess German diplomatic and consular staff.
subfiles.summary: Writing as Barton’s constituents and as members of the Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies, the Stettens urge him to press for a complete export embargo. They regard the reduction of German diplomatic and consular personnel as equally important.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bruce Barton concerning the Stetten letter
subfiles.about: The Department says the Stettens’ concerns are receiving close attention.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Barton’s October 15 forwarding letter and summarizes the issues as German diplomatic personnel and exports to Japan. It assures him that both matters are under close review and returns the constituent letter.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction to draft a reply
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hornbeck to prepare an appropriate reply to a pro-embargo correspondent.
subfiles.summary: The brief internal note directs Hornbeck to draft a response for Welles’s signature. It relates to the James Lawrence letter that follows.

subfiles.title: James Lawrence letter supporting a British-American embargo
subfiles.about: Lawrence endorses Major Eliot’s proposal for a complete British-American embargo on Japanese trade.
subfiles.summary: Lawrence says Eliot’s newspaper article makes compelling sense and prompts him to express support. Although he acknowledges limited knowledge of State Department problems and legislative authority, he hopes the Department’s influence will favor the proposed policy.

subfiles.title: Reply to James Lawrence
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges Lawrence’s support for a complete embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles says Lawrence’s views have received careful attention and thanks him for writing. He also acknowledges Lawrence’s good wishes and congratulations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: legal suit against Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum of conversation concerning litigation against Universal Oil Products Company.
subfiles.summary: The underlying conversation occurred with the Attorney General during discussion of amendments to the Export Control Act. The Attorney General expressed interest in the pending suit against Universal Oil Products.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: proposed scrap-iron embargo
subfiles.about: The sheet references a memorandum of conversation with the President about a proposed scrap-iron export embargo.
subfiles.summary: The original document is filed elsewhere in the Department’s records. The cross-reference identifies the subject as the proposed embargo on scrap-iron exports.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Welles–Japanese Ambassador conversation on export restrictions
subfiles.about: The sheet references a conversation about further restrictions on petroleum and scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary Welles discussed with the Japanese Ambassador a National Defense Advisory Council recommendation for tighter controls. The referenced original concerns petroleum products and scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Netherlands request concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Netherlands request that the United States avoid drastic export restrictions during negotiations in the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: The Netherlands chargé d’affaires asked that Washington refrain from severe curtailment while Japanese negotiations with local authorities continued. The original memorandum is filed under a different decimal classification.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products transmittal of Japan Gasoline Company requests
subfiles.from: Samuel S. Allender, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Allender submits three Japanese requests for refinery designs and notes that export-license applications have already been filed.
subfiles.summary: Universal Oil Products forwards copies of three September 17 letters signed by Japan Gasoline Company president Masao Saneyoshi. The requests concern designs, drawings, plans, and specifications allegedly due under agreements from 1928 and 1938. Allender says export-license applications numbered one through three cover the requested data.

subfiles.title: Japan Gasoline Company request for cracking and treating plant plans
subfiles.about: Japan Gasoline Company requests plans for motor-fuel cracking and treating plants licensed to Mitsui Mining and Fujinagata.
subfiles.summary: The company invokes its July 19, 1928 agreement to request designs, drawings, plans, and material specifications. It says the information is needed for agreements with Mitsui Mining Company and Fujinagata & Company and reserves its contractual right to seek further data and services.

subfiles.title: Japan Gasoline Company request for polymerization plant plans
subfiles.about: The company requests plans for catalytic polymerization plants in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Japan Gasoline Company says it has licensed non-selective catalytic polymerization processes to Mitsui Mining and the South Manchuria Railway Company. It asks when Universal Oil Products will dispatch the required designs and specifications while preserving its rights under existing agreements and pending litigation.

subfiles.title: Japan Gasoline Company request for multiple refinery-process designs
subfiles.about: The company requests extensive technical data for catalytic, hydrogenation, dehydrogenation, polymerization, isomerization, and alkylation plants.
subfiles.summary: The requested designs relate to projects for Chosen Oil, Toyo Shoko Oil, the Japanese government, Mitsui Mining, Mitsubishi Oil, and Nippon Oil in Japan and Korea. Japan Gasoline Company also anticipates needing data for isomerization, alkylation, and other processes. It asserts that the requests arise under the August 19, 1938 agreements and reserves its contractual and litigation rights.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese offer to purchase Bolivian tin
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report that Japan offered to buy Bolivian tin in exchange for arms and munitions.
subfiles.summary: Bolivia’s foreign minister reportedly hoped the United States could quickly resolve the tin-smelting question. The Japanese barter proposal linked strategic tin supplies to arms and ammunition.

subfiles.title: Antofagasta despatch on the Atlantico copper shipment
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Vice Consul at Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Adams reports that the Panamanian ship Atlantico is loading 7,500 tons of Chilean copper for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The copper cathodes come from the Chile Exploration Company’s Chuquicamata mine and are divided into lots for Osaka and Yokohama. No bills of lading are to be issued; the local representative will receive only the master’s receipts. The unprecedented size and unusual documentation of the shipment arouse suspicion about its ultimate destination.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting more information on the Atlantico
subfiles.about: The Department asks for any additional information available on the large copper shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The confidential telegram refers to despatch 105 of September 26. The consul is instructed to telegraph further findings about the Atlantico shipment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese order for lead at Monterrey
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report that an American company in Monterrey received a Japanese order for 1,000 tons of lead.
subfiles.summary: The underlying despatch is filed in another decimal series. The transaction concerns a large strategic-metal purchase for Japan from an American-operated Mexican company.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: E. Walter Earle letter on war-material embargo
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a separately filed letter concerning an embargo of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Only the subject, sender, date, and alternate file number appear here. The original communication is filed under decimal 893.51.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese purchases and tariff efforts in Costa Rica
subfiles.about: The sheet references Japanese attempts to buy Costa Rican scrap and remove a surcharge on Japanese imports.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui in New York offered to buy up to $10,000 in scrap rubber for shipment from Costa Rica to Japan. The minister asked whether the American position should be brought to President Calderón Guardia’s attention.

subfiles.title: Costa Rica despatch on Japanese scrap purchases and trade policy
subfiles.about: Hornibrook reports Japanese efforts to buy scrap rubber and metal while changing Costa Rica’s unfavorable trade balance.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui’s local agent, José Unckles, showed the legation a cable offering to purchase up to $10,000 of scrap rubber. Japan was also buying coffee and seeking other Costa Rican products so its goods could escape a 100 percent customs surcharge in 1941. Hornibrook asks whether American opposition to scrap exports to Japan should be raised with President Calderón Guardia.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: memorandum of interview with José Unckles
subfiles.about: Zweig records Mitsui agent José Unckles’s account of Japan’s campaign to improve its trade balance with Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: Unckles says Japan was reducing exports to Costa Rica and increasing purchases there to eliminate the 100 percent tariff surcharge on Japanese goods. He had instructions to acquire coffee, scrap rubber, and other usable products and had unsuccessfully urged President Calderón Guardia to buy Japanese cement. Unckles also discussed his Japanese, German, and Italian business connections and an employment offer from Amano in Panama.

subfiles.title: Santiago embassy despatch on the Atlantico
subfiles.about: Bowers supplies naval-attaché information about the ownership, fuel stop, and dual documentation of the Atlantico.
subfiles.summary: The Panamanian-registered vessel was expected to take fuel at Talara, Peru, and had formerly sailed under American registry as the Baltimore. It was reportedly purchased by Kitagawa Sangyo Kaiun of Osaka and would transfer to Japanese registry after reaching San Francisco. The ship was said to carry both Panamanian and Japanese papers.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: The Strategy of Rheostatic Control in Japanese Embargoes
subfiles.about: The sheet references three copies of an analysis on graduated control of embargoes against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The analysis was being sent to the Department by air mail. Its title suggests calibrated or rheostatic application of economic restrictions rather than a single absolute embargo.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Granby Copper Mine sales to Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses whether to investigate reports of a long-term Canadian copper contract with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Canadian Legation knew the Granby mine was selling copper to Japan but lacked specific information about an alleged three-year contract. Because American copper sales to Japan greatly exceeded Canadian sales and copper was not restricted by the United States, the memorandum concludes that seeking precise Canadian information would serve little purpose.

subfiles.title: H. J. Timperley letter on British and Canadian exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Timperley describes efforts in Britain to challenge trade with Japan and requests information about Granby copper sales.
subfiles.summary: Timperley says British parliamentarians are pressing their government to follow American controls on scrap metal and petroleum. He seeks facts about a reported three-year Granby Copper Mine contract so the matter can be raised in Parliament and with government offices. He also reports continued efforts to make British policy toward Japan politically uncomfortable.

subfiles.title: Hansard extract on Anglo-Iranian oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Members of Parliament question the British government about a million-barrel Anglo-Iranian oil sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Frederick Mander and other members argue that selling oil to Japan while closing the Burma Road unfairly aids the aggressor and penalizes China. Butler defends the government’s policy of not interfering with ordinary commercial activity but agrees to communicate the objections to the minister responsible for petroleum.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping on Canadian copper sales to Japan
subfiles.about: The clipping reports controversy over Granby copper exports to Japan and the Canadian government’s role.
subfiles.summary: The fragmented clipping records questions about whether the Canadian government had approved or been consulted on a copper contract. A Granby official is quoted as saying Britain had not requested the copper and that Japan was the company’s only other profitable market.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction to acknowledge Gardner’s letter
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hornbeck to acknowledge the enclosed pro-embargo letter.
subfiles.summary: The brief note forwards the correspondence for information. It directs Hornbeck to prepare an acknowledgment on Welles’s behalf.

subfiles.title: D. Z. Gardner letter supporting embargoes and British aid
subfiles.about: Gardner applauds restrictions on supplies to Japan and urges strong support for Britain.
subfiles.summary: Gardner argues that oil, scrap iron, and other materials sold to Japan could eventually be used against the United States. He expresses broader distrust of totalitarian states and some Latin American governments. He urges supporting Britain to the limit because it is fighting America’s battle.

subfiles.title: Reply to D. Z. Gardner
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Gardner’s letter on behalf of Sumner Welles.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that Gardner’s views have been carefully noted. He thanks Gardner for the spirit that prompted him to write.

subfiles.title: Warren A. Seavey letter advocating a comprehensive embargo
subfiles.about: Seavey argues for a complete embargo on Japan, substantial aid to China, and coordinated use of British bases.
subfiles.summary: Seavey contends that scrap restrictions alone will not prevent Japan from gaining other supplies or expanding toward China, British bases, and the Dutch East Indies. He argues that a complete trade embargo and substantial aid to China would weaken Japan and possibly stiffen Soviet resistance to Germany. He considers a major Japanese naval war unlikely or manageable and says the economic costs to the United States would be limited. He also maintains that American public opinion increasingly favors strong action even if it risks war.

subfiles.title: Berle reply to Warren A. Seavey
subfiles.about: Berle acknowledges Seavey’s proposals and says they have been circulated among interested State Department officers.
subfiles.summary: Berle thanks Seavey for his letter about the Far Eastern situation. He says its contents have been carefully noted and brought to the attention of other interested officials.

subfiles.title: Conversation with the Japanese Ambassador concerning Universal Oil Products
subfiles.about: Ambassador Horinouchi raises the unresolved Universal Oil Products matter and proposes a discussion with Counselor Morishima.
subfiles.summary: As he was leaving, Horinouchi noted that a question remained open concerning Universal Oil Products Corporation. He asked Berle to receive Morishima, and Berle agreed to see the counselor when he called.

subfiles.title: Antofagasta telegram reporting the Atlantico’s departure
subfiles.about: Adams reports that the Atlantico sailed for Japan with 7,600 long tons of copper cathodes.
subfiles.summary: The ship left Antofagasta on October 6 and was bound for Japan by way of San Pedro, California. The shipment had no bills of lading, only receipts issued by the master, and constituted the vessel’s entire cargo. Adams says a forthcoming airmail despatch will discuss other copper exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: First paraphrase of the Atlantico departure telegram
subfiles.about: The paraphrase restates the Atlantico’s cargo, route, and unusual documentation.
subfiles.summary: The Panamanian ship carried 7,600 tons of copper cathodes and no other cargo. It sailed for Japan via San Pedro with master’s receipts rather than bills of lading. Additional information on Japanese copper exports was being sent by air mail.

subfiles.title: Strictly confidential paraphrase of the Atlantico telegram
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Consulate at Antofagasta
subfiles.about: A second confidential paraphrase records the copper ship’s departure for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The document again states that the Atlantico sailed on October 6 with 7,600 long tons of copper cathodes. It emphasizes the absence of bills of lading, the exclusive copper cargo, and the route through San Pedro. It refers readers to a separate airmail despatch for other copper exports.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s request for advice on replying to MacLeish
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hornbeck what kind of reply should be sent to Archibald MacLeish.
subfiles.summary: The internal note refers to MacLeish’s transmittal of a Harvard group’s Far Eastern policy proposal. Welles requests Hornbeck’s views before responding.

subfiles.title: Archibald MacLeish letter forwarding a Far East proposal
subfiles.about: MacLeish sends Welles a memorandum proposing forceful American action in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: MacLeish acknowledges Welles’s heavy reading burden but believes the enclosure will interest him. The enclosure is the Harvard group memorandum reproduced on the following pages.

subfiles.title: The Far East: A Proposal for Action
subfiles.from: Warren A. Seavey and fourteen other members of a Harvard group
subfiles.about: The memorandum urges comprehensive economic and strategic action to prevent Japanese domination of China and the South Pacific.
subfiles.summary: The authors argue that an Axis-dominated Europe and a Japanese-dominated Far East would imperil American trade, hemispheric security, and the Monroe Doctrine. They propose embargoes on exports and imports involving Japan, extensive credits and munitions for Chiang Kai-shek’s government, and American use of Singapore and other British bases. They believe the United States still has naval superiority and can prevent Japan from conquering China or the Dutch East Indies. The final section asserts that recent events in Europe have awakened American public opinion and created support for vigorous action.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to Archibald MacLeish
subfiles.about: Welles thanks MacLeish for forwarding the Harvard group’s Far East memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Welles says that other copies of the proposal had already reached him. He assures MacLeish that the State Department has given its recommendations thoughtful consideration.
